title: Glaciers: Rivers of Ice
summary: How glaciers form from snow, flow slowly downhill, carve valleys, break into icebergs, store fresh water, and shrink as Earth warms.
poll: Glaciers far away from Saudi Arabia still matter to people who live here.

versions.title: Ice That Moves
versions.text:
Look at the high, cold hills. Do you see a big white sheet? It is a glacier. A glacier is a huge mass of ice.

How does it form? Snow falls on cold land. It does not all melt. More snow falls each year. The old snow gets pressed down. It turns to hard ice. This takes a long time.

A glacier is so big and so heavy that it moves. It slides down the hill. It is like a slow, slow river of ice.

As it moves, it scrapes the land. It drags big rocks. It digs a wide valley.

Some glaciers reach the sea. Big chunks break off. Each chunk is an iceberg.

Most of the fresh water on Earth is in ice. When ice melts, it fills streams. People drink that water. Farms use it too.

Now the world is warm. Lots of glaciers melt fast. They get small.

Long, long ago, ice was on land that is now Saudi Arabia!

versions.title: Ice That Moves
versions.text:
Look up at the tall, cold peaks. Do you see a thick white sheet? That is a glacier. A glacier is a huge mass of ice on land.

How does a glacier form? Snow falls where it is cold all year. Not all of it can melt in the short summer. So more snow piles up each year. The weight of the new snow packs the old snow down. Bit by bit, it turns to hard ice. This can take a hundred years.

A glacier is so thick and so heavy that it moves. Its own weight pulls it down the hill. It is like a slow river made of ice.

As it moves, a glacier scrapes the ground. It drags big rocks with it. Over a long time, it digs out a wide valley.

Some glaciers flow all the way to the sea. Big chunks crack off the end. Each chunk floats away as an iceberg.

Most of the fresh water on Earth is stored as ice. When ice melts in summer, it feeds streams and rivers. Lots of people drink this water. Farmers use it on their crops.

Today the world is getting warm. Many glaciers melt fast. New snow can not keep up. So they get small.

Long, long ago, thick ice sat on land that is now Saudi Arabia!

versions.title: Glaciers: Rivers of Ice
versions.text:
High on cold mountains, you may see a thick white sheet that seems to sit still. It is a glacier. A glacier is a huge mass of ice that lies on land.

How does a glacier form? Snow falls in places that stay cold all year. The short summer is not warm enough to melt all of it. So more snow piles up each year. The weight of the new snow presses the old snow down. Slowly, it turns into hard, thick ice. This can take a hundred years or more.

A glacier is so thick and so heavy that it moves. Its own weight pulls it downhill. That is why people call it a river of ice. Most glaciers move just a few steps a day.

As a glacier moves, it scrapes the ground below it. It drags rocks of all sizes with it. Over a very long time, it carves out a wide valley.

Some glaciers flow all the way to the sea. Huge chunks crack off the end and fall in the water. Each chunk floats away as an iceberg.

Most of the fresh water on Earth is stored as ice. In summer, melting ice feeds streams and rivers. Millions of people drink this water, and farmers use it for their crops.

Today Earth is getting warmer. Many glaciers melt faster than new snow can build them up, so they are shrinking.

Long, long ago, thick ice even covered land that is now part of Saudi Arabia. Scientists can still see scratches it left on the rocks!

versions.title: Glaciers: Rivers of Ice
versions.text:
High on cold mountains, you may spot a thick white sheet that seems to sit perfectly still. It is a glacier, a huge mass of ice that lies on land. Even though it looks frozen in place, it is always moving.

A glacier begins with snow. In some places, it stays cold all year, and the short summer is not warm enough to melt all the snow. So more snow piles up each winter. The weight of the new layers presses the old snow down until it turns into hard, thick ice. This can take a hundred years or more.

A glacier is so thick and so heavy that its own weight pulls it slowly downhill. That is why people call it a river of ice. Most glaciers creep forward just a few steps each day.

As a glacier moves, it scrapes the ground beneath it and drags along rocks of every size. Over thousands of years, it carves out a wide valley with steep sides.

Some glaciers flow all the way to the sea. Huge chunks crack off the front and crash into the water. Each chunk floats away as an iceberg.

Most of the fresh water on Earth is stored as ice. In summer, melting glaciers feed streams and rivers. Millions of people drink this water, and farmers use it to grow crops.

Today Earth is getting warmer, and many glaciers melt faster than new snow can build them up. As a result, they are shrinking.

Long ago, thick ice even covered land that is now part of Saudi Arabia. Scientists can still find scratches it left on the rocks.

versions.title: Glaciers: Rivers of Ice
versions.text:
High in cold mountains, you may notice a massive white sheet that seems to sit perfectly still. It is a glacier, a huge body of ice that rests on land. Although it looks frozen in place, a glacier is always on the move.

Every glacier begins as snow. In some places, the weather stays cold for most of the year, and the short summer cannot melt all the snow that fell in winter. Year after year, new layers pile on top. Their weight starts to compress the older snow beneath them, squeezing out the air until it becomes solid, dense ice. This process can take a century or longer.

Once the ice grows thick enough, its own weight pulls it slowly downhill. For this reason, people often call a glacier a river of ice. Most glaciers creep forward only a few centimeters or meters each day.

As it moves, a glacier acts like a giant file. It scrapes the ground beneath it and carries rocks, sand, and other debris along. Over thousands of years, it can carve a deep valley with steep walls.

Some glaciers flow all the way to the ocean. There, enormous chunks crack off the front and crash into the water. Scientists call this calving, and each floating chunk is an iceberg.

Glaciers also store most of the fresh water on Earth. In warm months, melting ice feeds streams and rivers. They supply drinking water to millions of people and help farmers grow crops.

Today, however, Earth is warming, and many glaciers are melting faster than new snow can replace them. As they shrink, the extra water flows into the sea and raises its level.

Long ago, thick ice even covered land that is now part of Saudi Arabia. Scientists can still find scratches it left on ancient rocks.

versions.title: Glaciers: Rivers of Ice
versions.text:
High in frozen mountain ranges, you may notice a massive white sheet that appears to rest perfectly motionless. It is a glacier, an enormous body of ice lying on land. Although it seems permanently fixed in place, a glacier is continuously moving, and over long periods it dramatically reshapes the surrounding landscape.

Every glacier originates as ordinary snow. In certain regions, temperatures remain cold for most of the year, so the brief summer cannot melt all the snow that fell during winter. As layers accumulate year after year, their increasing weight compresses the older snow beneath them. The trapped air is gradually squeezed out, and the snow becomes grainy and eventually solid, dense ice, a transformation that can require a century or longer. Exceptionally dense glacial ice often appears blue, because it absorbs red light while reflecting blue light.

Glaciers occur in two principal forms. Mountain glaciers occupy high valleys, whereas ice sheets spread across entire landmasses, such as Antarctica and Greenland. Once the ice becomes sufficiently thick, its tremendous weight pulls it slowly downhill or outward, which is why people describe a glacier as a river of ice. Most glaciers advance only a few centimeters or meters each day, although certain glaciers travel considerably faster.

As it moves, a glacier functions like a gigantic file, scraping the ground beneath it and transporting rocks, gravel, and other debris along its path. Through this erosion, a glacier can gradually carve a narrow river valley into a broad U shape. Where the ice eventually melts, it deposits long ridges of rock and sediment called moraines.

Some glaciers flow all the way to the ocean. At their edge, enormous chunks fracture and plunge into the water, a process that scientists call calving, and each floating chunk becomes an iceberg.

Glaciers and ice sheets contain roughly two-thirds of the fresh water on Earth, so they function as a vast frozen reservoir. During warm months, melting ice nourishes streams and rivers that supply drinking water for millions of people and irrigate valuable agricultural land.

Today, however, Earth's climate is warming, and numerous glaciers are melting faster than new snowfall can replace them. As they shrink, the additional water drains into the ocean and gradually raises global sea levels.

Remarkably, thick ice once covered territory that is now part of Saudi Arabia, approximately 450 million years ago, and geologists can still identify the scratches it carved into ancient rocks.

versions.text:

It is a glacier, an enormous body of ice situated on land, and although it seems permanently fixed in place, a glacier is continuously moving, dramatically reshaping the surrounding landscape over extended periods.

Every glacier originates as ordinary snow. In certain regions, temperatures remain cold for most of the year, so the brief summer cannot melt all the snow that accumulated during the preceding winter. As layers accumulate year after year, their increasing weight compresses the older snow beneath them, progressively squeezing out the trapped air until the snow becomes granular and eventually solid, exceptionally dense ice, a transformation that can require a century or longer. Such compacted glacial ice frequently appears blue, because it absorbs the red wavelengths of visible light while reflecting the blue ones.

Glaciers occur in two principal forms. Mountain glaciers occupy elevated valleys, whereas ice sheets spread across entire landmasses, such as Antarctica and Greenland. Once the ice becomes sufficiently thick, its tremendous weight pulls it gradually downhill or outward, which explains why people characterize a glacier as a river of ice. Most glaciers advance only a few centimeters or meters each day, although certain glaciers travel considerably faster.

As it moves, a glacier functions like a gigantic file, abrading the underlying bedrock and transporting rocks, gravel, and other debris along its path. Through this relentless erosion, a glacier can gradually transform a narrow river valley into a broad U shape, and where the ice eventually melts, it deposits elongated ridges of rock and sediment called moraines.

Some glaciers flow all the way to the ocean, where enormous chunks fracture and plunge into the water, a process that scientists call calving, and each floating fragment becomes an independent iceberg.

Glaciers and ice sheets collectively contain approximately two-thirds of the fresh water on Earth, so they function as an immense frozen reservoir. During warm months, melting ice nourishes streams and rivers that supply drinking water for millions of people and irrigate valuable agricultural land throughout the surrounding regions.

Today, however, Earth's climate is warming, and numerous glaciers are melting considerably faster than new snowfall can replenish them. As they shrink, the additional meltwater drains into the ocean and gradually contributes to rising global sea levels, which threaten low-lying coastal communities.

Remarkably, thick ice once covered territory that is now part of Saudi Arabia, approximately 450 million years ago, when that region lay near the South Pole, and geologists can still identify the distinctive scratches it carved into ancient rocks.

keyWords.definition: a huge, thick mass of ice on land that moves very slowly
keyWords.example: The climbers took photos of the glacier from the top of the mountain.

keyWords.definition: to change from something solid, like ice, into a liquid, like water
keyWords.example: Put the chocolate in the sun and it will melt.

keyWords.definition: low land between hills or mountains
keyWords.example: We could see a small village down in the valley.

keyWords.definition: a very big piece of ice that floats in the sea
keyWords.example: Most of an iceberg is hidden under the water.

keyWords.definition: (of water) not salty, so people can drink it
keyWords.example: The camp had a well with clean, fresh water.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How to stay warm on a snowy mountain
How glaciers form, move, and matter
Why icebergs are dangerous for ships
How people make ice in a freezer
questions.why: The whole article explains what a glacier is, how it forms from snow, how it moves and shapes land, and why its water is important.

wrong.A: The article does not give tips for staying warm.
wrong.C: Icebergs are only one small part, and ships are not mentioned.
wrong.D: The article is about natural ice on land, not freezers.

questions.stem: What is a glacier made from?
options: Salty sea water that froze solid on the shore
Rain that turned to hail
Snow that piled up and was pressed into ice
Rocks that got covered with a thin layer of frost
questions.why: The article says snow piles up each year, the old snow gets pressed down, and it turns to hard ice.

wrong.A: The article says glaciers form on land from snow, not from sea water.
wrong.B: Hail is not mentioned in the article.
wrong.D: Glaciers carry rocks, but they are made of ice from snow.

questions.stem: What happens when a big chunk breaks off a glacier at the sea?
options: It becomes an iceberg.
It turns into snow.
It sinks to the bottom.
It makes a new valley.
questions.why: The article says big chunks break off where glaciers reach the sea, and each chunk is an iceberg.

wrong.B: Ice does not turn back into snow in the article.
wrong.C: The article says the chunks float, not sink.
wrong.D: Glaciers dig valleys on land as they move, not when chunks break off.

questions.stem: Why does a glacier move?
options: Strong winds push it across the land.
Camels and other animals drag it along.
Heavy rain washes it down into the sea.
It is so heavy that its weight pulls it downhill.
questions.why: The article says a glacier is so big and heavy that it moves down the hill.

wrong.A: Wind is not given as the reason a glacier moves.
wrong.B: No animals move glaciers in the article.
wrong.C: Rain is not the reason; the glacier's own weight is.

questions.stem: The article says a glacier is like a slow river of ice. What does this comparison help you understand?
options: Glaciers are full of fish that swim downhill.
A glacier flows downhill, but very slowly.
Glaciers are made of warm water.
A glacier moves as fast as a river.
questions.why: A river flows downhill. Calling a glacier a SLOW river shows it also flows downhill, only much more slowly.

wrong.A: The comparison is about moving, not about fish.
wrong.C: Glaciers are made of ice, not warm water.
wrong.D: The word 'slow' tells us it does not move as fast as a river.

questions.stem: What can you tell from the fact that people drink water from melting glaciers?
options: Some people may have less water later.
Glacier water is too salty to drink.
Only people in Saudi Arabia need glaciers.
People should stop using rivers.
questions.why: Melting ice fills streams that people drink from and farms use. If glaciers shrink, there may be less of this water later.

wrong.B: The article says glaciers hold fresh water, which is not salty.
wrong.C: The article does not say this; many people around the world use the water.
wrong.D: The article never tells people to stop using rivers.

questions.stem: Read this: "As it moves, it scrapes the land." What does scrapes mean here?
options: Paints in bright colors
Jumps up and over the top
Waters gently
Rubs hard against and wears away
questions.why: The glacier rubs hard on the ground and drags rocks, which is how it digs a valley.

wrong.A: A glacier does not paint anything.
wrong.B: A glacier stays on the ground; it does not jump.
wrong.C: The sentence is about rubbing the land, not watering it.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the article with the fact about ice long ago in Saudi Arabia?
options: To explain how to make honey
To prove that glaciers are moving to Saudi Arabia now
To link glaciers to the reader's own land
To teach how icebergs float
questions.why: It is a surprising fact that connects a far-away topic to the reader's own country.

wrong.A: Honey is not part of this article.
wrong.B: The article says this happened long, long ago, not now.
wrong.D: Icebergs are explained earlier, not in the last paragraph.

LOW.prompt: Explain in your own words how a glacier forms and how it changes the land. Use at least two facts from the article.
checklist: I explained how snow turns into a glacier.
I told one way a glacier changes the land.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: A glacier forms when snow piles up year after year and its weight squeezes the layers into solid ice. Once the glacier is heavy enough, it slowly starts to melt and slide downhill. As it moves, it scrapes the ground and carves out a deep valley. When a glacier reaches the ocean, pieces break off and float away as an iceberg.

keyWords.definition: to press something together so it takes up less space
keyWords.example: He had to compress his clothes to fit them all in the bag.

keyWords.definition: broken pieces of rock, wood, or other things that are left or carried along
keyWords.example: After the storm, workers cleared the debris from the road.

keyWords.definition: when large pieces of ice break off the edge of a glacier into water
keyWords.example: The visitors heard a loud crack and watched calving at the edge of the ice.

keyWords.definition: to cut or shape something by slowly removing parts of it
keyWords.example: The artist used a small knife to carve a camel out of wood.
A wool sweater may shrink if you wash it in hot water.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?
options: Glaciers never change and always stay in one place on a mountain.
Icebergs are the largest and most dangerous objects in the whole ocean.
Glaciers form from snow, shape land, store water, and are shrinking.
Snow is only found on the highest mountains, far away from people.
questions.why: The article covers how glaciers form, move, carve land, hold fresh water, and melt as Earth warms.

wrong.A: The article says glaciers are always moving and are shrinking.
wrong.B: The article does not compare iceberg sizes with other objects.
wrong.D: This is not the article's main point, and it is not stated.

questions.stem: According to the article, how long can it take for snow to become glacier ice?
options: A century or longer
About one winter
A few weeks in spring
Exactly ten years
questions.why: The article says the change from snow to dense ice can take a century or longer.

wrong.B: One winter is far too short; the snow must pile up over many years.
wrong.C: A few weeks is not mentioned and is much too short.
wrong.D: The article does not give ten years.

questions.stem: What happens to the air in the snow as a glacier forms?
options: It turns into water vapor and rises.
It is squeezed out by the weight of new layers.
It freezes into bubbles that make the ice float.
It stays inside and makes the ice soft.
questions.why: The article says the weight of new layers compresses the old snow and squeezes out the air.

wrong.A: The article does not say the air becomes vapor.
wrong.D: The ice becomes solid and dense, not soft.

questions.stem: Which event happens FIRST in the life of a glacier?
options: Large chunks break off and fall into the ocean.
The moving ice carves a deep valley in the land.
The thick ice begins to slide slowly downhill.
Snow piles up because summer cannot melt it all.
questions.why: A glacier begins as snow that piles up year after year; moving, carving, and calving all happen later.

wrong.A: Calving happens only after the glacier has moved to the sea.
wrong.B: Carving happens as the glacier moves, which comes later.
wrong.C: The ice must first become thick enough before it moves.

questions.stem: Read this: "a glacier acts like a giant file." A file is a tool used to rub and smooth surfaces. What does this comparison suggest?
options: A glacier slowly grinds and wears down the ground.
A glacier stores papers and records.
A glacier is sharp enough to cut people.
A glacier is small enough to hold in your hand.
questions.why: Like a file rubbing a surface, the glacier scrapes and grinds the land, carving valleys.

wrong.B: This is a different meaning of 'file' that does not fit the sentence.
wrong.C: The article does not say glaciers cut people.
wrong.D: Glaciers are described as huge, not small.

questions.stem: Why might a valley in a place with no ice today still show signs of a glacier?
options: Because rain always makes deep valleys
Because icebergs float into valleys
A glacier melted long ago may have carved it.
Because glaciers can only form in deserts
questions.why: The article says glaciers carve valleys and that scientists find scratches from ancient ice in Saudi Arabia, so marks can remain after the ice is gone.

wrong.A: The article does not say rain always makes deep valleys.
wrong.B: Icebergs float in the sea, not into valleys.
wrong.D: Glaciers form where it stays cold, not in deserts.

questions.stem: Based on the article, what could happen to sea levels if glaciers keep melting quickly?
options: They would fall.
They would rise.
They would stay exactly the same.
They would freeze solid.
questions.why: The article says water from shrinking glaciers flows into the sea and raises its level, so more melting means higher seas.

wrong.A: Adding water makes the sea rise, not fall.
wrong.D: A warming Earth would not freeze the sea solid.

questions.stem: How does the author mainly organize the article?
options: As a story about one family on a trip to the mountains
As a list of rules for mountain climbers
By comparing glaciers with deserts in each paragraph
By telling the life of a glacier, from snow to melting
questions.why: The paragraphs move in order: how a glacier starts, how it moves, what it does to land and sea, and how it melts.

wrong.A: There is no family or trip in the article.
wrong.B: The article gives information, not rules.

MID.prompt: Explain how glaciers help people and why melting glaciers are a problem. Use details from the article.
checklist: I explained at least one way glaciers help people.
I explained at least one problem caused by melting glaciers.
I used details from the article to support my ideas.
MID.modelAnswer: Glaciers help people because they store fresh water, and melting ice in warm months feeds streams and rivers that give drinking water and irrigation to millions of people. But melting glaciers also cause a problem: when they shrink faster than new snow can replace them, the extra water drains into the sea and raises its level. Over thousands of years glaciers also carve valleys and carry debris downhill, showing how differently they change the land compared to how quickly they are melting today.

keyWords.definition: to gather or pile up little by little over time
keyWords.example: Dust will accumulate on the shelf if no one cleans it.

keyWords.definition: the slow wearing away of land or rock by water, wind, or ice
keyWords.example: Trees planted along the hill help stop erosion of the soil.

keyWords.definition: a long pile of rocks and soil left behind by a glacier
keyWords.example: The hikers walked along a rocky moraine at the end of the old glacier.

keyWords.definition: a place where a large supply of water is stored
keyWords.example: The city gets its tap water from a reservoir behind the dam.

keyWords.definition: the breaking off of large chunks of ice from the edge of a glacier into water
keyWords.example: Scientists filmed the calving from a boat at a safe distance.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Ice sheets in Antarctica are much larger and older than the ice sheets in Greenland.
Glaciers shape land, store fresh water, and are shrinking as Earth warms.
Blue ice is the most valuable kind of glacier ice, so scientists collect it.
Moraines are the most important landform on Earth.
questions.why: This statement covers the main threads of the article: formation and movement, effects on the land, water storage, and melting.

wrong.A: The article does not compare the sizes of the two ice sheets.
wrong.C: Blue ice is a minor detail, and 'valuable' is never claimed.
wrong.D: Moraines are one detail, not the central idea.

questions.stem: According to the article, why does very dense glacial ice often look blue?
options: It contains blue minerals from rocks.
It reflects the color of the sky above it.
It absorbs red light and reflects blue light.
It is colder than other kinds of ice.
questions.why: The article explains that dense ice absorbs red light while reflecting blue light.

wrong.A: Minerals are not given as the cause of the color.
wrong.B: The sky is not mentioned as the reason.
wrong.D: Temperature is not linked to the blue color.

questions.stem: Which two forms of glaciers does the article describe?
options: Mountain glaciers and ice sheets
Icebergs and moraines
Sea glaciers and desert glaciers
Snow glaciers and rain glaciers
questions.why: The article names mountain glaciers in high valleys and ice sheets that cover landmasses such as Antarctica and Greenland.

wrong.B: Icebergs and moraines are things glaciers produce, not forms of glaciers.
wrong.C: The article mentions no desert glaciers.
wrong.D: These categories are not in the article.

questions.stem: What is the result of glacial erosion on a narrow river valley?
options: It fills the valley with sea water.
It turns the valley into a desert.
It freezes the river so it can never flow again.
It widens the valley into a broad U shape.
questions.why: The article states that through erosion a glacier can carve a narrow river valley into a broad U shape.

wrong.A: Sea water is not part of this process.
wrong.B: The article does not connect erosion to deserts.
wrong.C: Freezing the river forever is not described.

questions.stem: In the article, glaciers are called a vast frozen "reservoir." What does this word choice suggest?
options: Glaciers are dangerous places for people to approach.
Glaciers store water that is released over time.
Glaciers are man-made structures.
Glaciers contain mostly salt water.
questions.why: A reservoir stores water for later use; glaciers hold fresh water that melts into rivers during warm months.

wrong.A: Danger is not what the word suggests.
wrong.C: Glaciers are natural, even though many reservoirs are built by people.
wrong.D: The article says glaciers hold fresh water.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the fact that thick ice once covered land that is now part of Saudi Arabia?
options: To argue that large glaciers will soon return to cover Saudi Arabia
To show that Saudi Arabia has some of the largest glaciers in the world today
To show that climates change over time and link the topic to readers
To explain how icebergs are formed
questions.why: The detail reveals that even a hot desert region once had glaciers, showing change over time and linking the subject to Saudi readers.

wrong.A: The article makes no prediction that glaciers will return.
wrong.B: The article does not say Saudi Arabia has glaciers today.
wrong.D: Iceberg formation is explained in a different paragraph.

questions.stem: A scientist finds a long ridge of mixed rocks and gravel in a valley where there is no ice today. What can she most reasonably conclude?
options: A glacier probably once melted there and left a moraine.
An iceberg floated into the valley quite recently.
A fast river carried all the rocks up the hill.
The rocks were dropped there by calving at the sea.
questions.why: The article says glaciers transport rock debris and, where the ice melts, deposit ridges called moraines.

wrong.B: Icebergs float in the ocean, not into dry valleys.
wrong.C: Rivers do not carry rocks uphill, and this is not mentioned.
wrong.D: Calving happens at the ocean edge and creates icebergs, not ridges.

questions.stem: Based on the article, why could people far from any glacier still be affected by glacier melting?
options: Melting glaciers make the air much too cold in every country.
Melting glaciers stop snow from falling anywhere else in the world.
Melting glaciers turn rivers everywhere into solid sheets of ice.
Meltwater raises global sea levels, which affects coasts everywhere.
questions.why: The article explains that water from shrinking glaciers drains into the ocean and raises global sea levels, an effect that reaches far beyond the mountains.

wrong.A: Melting is linked to warming, not to colder air.
wrong.B: The article does not say melting stops snowfall worldwide.
wrong.C: Melting produces more liquid water, not frozen rivers.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says glaciers far from Saudi Arabia still matter to people here. Do you agree? Write a paragraph that uses at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
checklist: I stated a clear opinion about the poll statement.
I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how each piece of evidence connects to my opinion.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that glaciers far from Saudi Arabia still matter to people here. Glaciers act like a giant reservoir, since centuries of snow accumulate and then melt into streams and rivers that millions of people depend on for drinking water and irrigation, even if they live nowhere near the ice. As these glaciers shrink faster than fresh snow can replace them, the extra meltwater raises sea levels everywhere, including coastlines close to the Kingdom. Even though no glacier exists here today, thick ice once covered land that is now part of Saudi Arabia, and the erosion scars it left in ancient rocks show that what happens to distant glaciers has always been connected to us.
